lesson.title: Why Solids Hold Their Shape
lesson.summary: A solid keeps a fixed shape and volume because its particles are locked into place, close enough together for strong intermolecular or bonding forces to overpower their thermal motion almost entirely.
lesson.body:
A solid is the state of matter in which particles are packed closely together in essentially fixed positions, able to vibrate in place but not to move freely past one another. This fixed arrangement is why solids have both a definite shape and a definite volume that do not change when the container changes, unlike liquids or gases. The particles in a solid are typically packed about as closely as physically possible given their size and shape, which is also why solids generally have higher densities than the liquid or gas forms of the same substance, with water being a well known exception because of how hydrogen bonding arranges ice into an unusually open lattice.

The reason particles stay locked in place comes directly from the competition described in states of matter: in a solid, the attractive forces holding particles together, whether intermolecular forces like dispersion, dipole-dipole, or hydrogen bonding, or stronger bonding forces like ionic or metallic bonding, are large relative to the particles' kinetic energy at that temperature. Each particle still vibrates around a fixed average position, since it retains some kinetic energy, but it does not have enough energy to break free of its neighbors and migrate through the material, which is exactly what would happen if it were melting into a liquid.

The strength of the forces holding a solid together varies enormously depending on what those forces actually are, and this variation shows up directly in melting points. A solid held together mainly by weak London dispersion forces, like solid carbon dioxide, dry ice, melts (sublimes, in that particular case) at a low temperature, around minus 78 degrees Celsius, because comparatively little thermal energy is needed to overcome such weak attractions. A solid held together by strong ionic bonds, like sodium chloride, melts only at 801 degrees Celsius, since ionic bonds are far stronger than dispersion forces and require much more thermal energy to break. A covalent network solid like diamond, in which every carbon atom is joined to its neighbors by covalent bonds throughout the entire crystal, melts above 3500 degrees Celsius, reflecting just how strong covalent bonding is compared to any purely intermolecular force.

Because the identity and strength of the forces holding particles in place can differ so much from one solid to the next, solids are usually sorted into subtypes based on those forces and on the internal arrangement of their particles. The two broadest categories are crystalline solids, in which particles are arranged in a highly ordered, repeating pattern, and amorphous solids, in which particles are arranged with no long-range order at all. Both categories still fit the basic definition of a solid, fixed shape and fixed volume from immobilized particles, but the degree of internal order, and the way each type responds to heating, differs substantially between them, which is worth examining separately.
